angle: Backend/API Architecture — workers/ai-proxy, apps/api, workers/cron, workers/apns-push, packages/worker-http
angleSummary: The ai-proxy worker exposes two unauthenticated Anthropic API proxy endpoints (/brain-dump and /v1/messages) that are rate-limited only by a spoofable client-supplied header, creating direct financial exposure. A misleading wrangler.toml queue binding comment masks an either-deploy-breaking-or-double-processing defect. Several lower-severity analytic, rate-limit, and auth issues round out the picture.

mergedFindings.title: /brain-dump and /v1/messages are unauthenticated Anthropic API proxies — ANTHROPIC_API_KEY freely abusable
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/index.ts lines 436-510: after all route matches, the /brain-dump and /v1/messages paths proceed to the Anthropic proxy with ZERO JWT verification. The rate-limit key is `rl:ai:${userKey}` where userKey = req.headers.get('x-user-id') || cf-connecting-ip || 'anon' — all three are caller-controlled. Code confirmed at runtime via direct read: the fetch to ANTHROPIC_URL at the end of the handler has no verifyClerkJwt guard. The worker URL is embedded in packages/api/src/anthropic.ts line 142 as a public constant. /route/dump (same file, line ~391) already has verifyClerkJwt — the contrast makes the gap unambiguous.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Any internet caller who discovers the CF worker URL can burn ANTHROPIC_API_KEY credits at 10 req/min per spoofed x-user-id value. With 100 rotating IDs = 1000 req/min potential drain. Service disruption and financial liability for Serra's Anthropic account. No user data leaks (bodies are proxied, not stored), but a sustained attack could suspend the API key and take down all AI features.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Financial cost runaway with no audit trail. The unauthenticated path also caches responses in CACHE_KV keyed by body hash, meaning adversary requests can poison the AI response cache.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add `const sub = await verifyClerkJwt(bearer, env); if (!sub) return withCors(origin, json({ error: 'unauthorized' }, 401));` at the top of the /brain-dump+/v1/messages block, matching the pattern already used in dump.ts. Add T0_JWT_ENFORCED !== '0' dev escape hatch. Coordinate with packages/api/src/anthropic.ts callers to ensure Clerk JWT is forwarded.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Breaking change for callers not yet sending Clerk JWT. Audit packages/api/src/anthropic.ts caller sites first. The cron drain (workers/cron/src/drain.ts line 240) calls /v1/messages via service binding with x-user-id: cron-drain — needs to switch to a pre-shared internal secret or move to /route/dump.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: workers/ai-proxy/tests/clerk-verify.test.ts: POST /brain-dump with no Authorization → 401; POST /brain-dump with forged x-user-id only → 401; POST /brain-dump with valid Clerk JWT → 200.

mergedFindings.title: [[queues.producers]] and [[queues.consumers]] blocks are ACTIVE in wrangler.toml despite comment saying 'intentionally left commented' — next CI deploy fails or enrichment double-processes
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/wrangler.toml lines 73-81: comment at lines 73-75 says the block must be commented out if ollie-enrich-queue is not provisioned, then lines 79-81 have an ACTIVE (uncommented) [[queues.producers]] binding with queue = 'ollie-enrich-queue'. Same in workers/cron/wrangler.toml lines 58-63: [[queues.consumers]] is also active. If the queue does not exist in CF, wrangler deploy fails for both workers blocking all CI pushes. If the queue DOES exist, Round 3 raises a second problem: cron/src/index.ts scheduled() still calls drainEnrichQueue via the 5-min KV scan path (line 126 comment confirms both paths are live), meaning every dump processed by the Queue consumer is also re-processed by the KV scan — double AI calls + potential duplicate enriched_signals rows.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Either: (a) next push to main breaks CI deploy for ai-proxy and cron, meaning no security fixes ship, OR (b) if queue is provisioned, every brain dump enrichment runs twice — double Anthropic cost + analytics double-counting.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: CI/CD reliability and enrichment correctness. Wrangler errors on binding resolution before the worker boots if queue is missing.
mergedFindings.dissent: Round 1 and Round 2 treat this primarily as a CI/deploy risk (queue not provisioned). Round 3 adds a second failure mode: if the queue IS provisioned, the KV drain cron still runs simultaneously, creating double-processing. Both risk paths are real and not mutually exclusive.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Run `wrangler queues list` to determine which scenario applies. If queue NOT provisioned: comment out the [[queues.producers]] block in ai-proxy/wrangler.toml and [[queues.consumers]] in cron/wrangler.toml to restore working KV-drain path. If queue IS provisioned: disable the `enrich-drain` branch in cron/src/index.ts scheduled() (the queue consumer owns it now). Fix the misleading comment either way.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Medium — must verify queue existence before picking the fix branch. Code already has `if (env.ENRICH_QUEUE)` guard, making either path safe once TOML is consistent.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: CI step: `wrangler deploy --dry-run` to catch binding resolution errors before real deploy. Add a test asserting drainEnrichQueue is NOT called from scheduled() when ENRICH_QUEUE binding is present.

mergedFindings.title: cacheHitUpdate sends `{ hit_count: { increment: 1 } }` to PostgREST PATCH — invalid syntax, silently fails on every cache hit
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/router/route.ts line 448: `body: JSON.stringify({ hit_count: { increment: 1 }, last_hit_at: ... })`. PostgREST PATCH performs a JSON merge-replace — `{ increment: 1 }` is an object literal, not an integer. The column is `int not null` (confirmed in migration 20260521000001_routing_cache.sql). PostgREST returns a 400 type-mismatch which is silently swallowed by the fire-and-forget .catch(). Round 3 also identifies the same bug in workers/ai-proxy/src/router/feed-me.ts line 818. route.test.ts at lines 230-244 mocks the PATCH to 204 without validating the body — the test never caught this. The `{ increment: N }` syntax is a Supabase JS client v2 ORM sugar; it is NOT supported by the raw REST endpoint.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Invisible to users — routing and cache returns still work. hit_count is permanently 0 for all routing_cache rows. Cache eviction scoring (evictionScore uses hit_count) degrades: popular entries may be evicted while cold entries survive, making AI routing slower for repeat inputs over time.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: routing_cache.hit_count permanently 0. Same bug in feed-me.ts. Fire-and-forget means no alerting. Test suite passes despite guaranteed runtime failure.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add migration: `CREATE FUNCTION routing_cache_increment_hit(p_id uuid) RETURNS void LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER AS $$ UPDATE routing_cache SET hit_count = hit_count + 1, last_hit_at = now() WHERE id = p_id $$;` Then replace the PATCH call with `fetch(rest(env, 'rpc/routing_cache_increment_hit'), { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({ p_id: id }) })`. Apply the same fix in feed-me.ts.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low — purely additive migration and a 5-line TS change. No schema change needed.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Assert PATCH body on cache hit has hit_count as a number not an object. Add test asserting the RPC endpoint is called with the correct id.

mergedFindings.title: /validate-invite and /claim-invite have no application-level rate limit — invite code enumeration possible
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/index.ts lines 376-381: /validate-invite and /claim-invite dispatch with no checkRate() call. workers/ai-proxy/src/invites.ts line 20-21 comment confirms this: 'Validate and claim are not user-rate-limited but rely on the per-IP CF rate limit.' /validate-invite returns distinct error reasons: 'not_found', 'used', 'expired' (lines 199, 201, 205) which enable oracle-based enumeration. CF free-tier default is ~10k req/min per IP — far above a useful threshold.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Attacker with multiple IPs can enumerate and claim invite codes intended for Serra's network, locking legitimate users out. An adversary claiming codes can exhaust the invite pool.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: No server-side failed-attempt counter means no signal for throttling or alerting. Distinct error messages make enumeration easier than a single-response approach.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add `checkRate(env.TELEM_RATE_LIMITER, env.RATE_KV, 'rl:validate:' + (req.headers.get('cf-connecting-ip') ?? 'anon'), 20)` before the validate/claim handlers. Same pattern used elsewhere — ~5 lines each. Optionally collapse not_found/used/expired to a single `{ valid: false }` to remove the oracle.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Negligible — validate is called once per user sign-up flow. 20/min per IP is generous for legitimate use.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: workers/ai-proxy/tests/invites.test.ts: assert /validate-invite returns 429 after N rapid calls from same IP.

mergedFindings.title: resolveUserIdForRateLimit falls through to spoofable x-user-id header when Clerk JWT is absent — rate-limit key is forgeable
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/index.ts lines 520-536 (resolveUserIdForRateLimit): if T0_JWT_ENFORCED is active but Clerk JWT verification returns null, the function falls through to `req.headers.get('x-user-id')` — a caller-supplied, unverified header. Applied to /grocery/purchase, /cook-history, /transcribe, /partner/*, /feed-me, /shelf-life. The handlers themselves enforce JWT and will 401, but the rate-limit bucket is assigned BEFORE the auth check and uses the spoofed key. An attacker with a working account can bypass per-user caps by rotating x-user-id values on /transcribe (Groq Whisper budget) and /feed-me (Voyage+Groq budget).
mergedFindings.userImpact: AI cost controls weakened for Whisper and Voyage+Groq paths. An authenticated user can effectively multiply their quota by rotating x-user-id values.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Rate-limit bypass for Groq Whisper and Voyage+Groq endpoints. The 401 still fires, but the rate-limit counter is recorded under a fake key, not the real user's bucket.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: In resolveUserIdForRateLimit: only return a non-null key if Clerk JWT verified successfully. If verification fails and T0_JWT_ENFORCED is active, return null — the handler will 401 before any rate-limited resource is consumed. Remove the x-user-id fallback from the rate-limit key path when JWT enforcement is active.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low. Handlers already 401 unauthenticated callers. The rate-limit key just needs to be consistent with the auth decision.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Test that a request with invalid JWT and custom x-user-id is NOT counted under that x-user-id bucket after the fix.

mergedFindings.title: Groq fetch in groq.ts has no AbortController timeout — hung Groq response holds CF Worker slot for up to 30s wall-clock
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/groq.ts line 102: `const res = await fetch(GROQ_URL, { method: 'POST', headers: {...}, body: JSON.stringify(body) })` — no AbortController, no timeout signal. grep confirms no AbortController or signal in groq.ts. The tier ladder in route.ts (lines 528-568 per Round 2) can call groqClassify twice on a cache miss (cheap model then expensive), doubling latency exposure. CF Worker wall-clock limit is 30s; a hung Groq call silently saturates it. No retry-after signal is returned to the client.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Dump submission appears to hang for up to 30s when Groq is slow or down. User sees an indefinite spinner. After 30s CF returns a 502 with no retry hint to the client.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: No observable failure signal for Groq timeouts. Worker CPU slot held for 30s, blocking concurrent requests in the same isolate. No circuit-breaker or deterministic fallback deadline violates the Layer 1 harness contract (timing = deterministic harness, not LLM path).
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Wrap the Groq fetch in an AbortController with a 10s deadline: `const ac = new AbortController(); setTimeout(() => ac.abort(), 10_000); const res = await fetch(GROQ_URL, { ..., signal: ac.signal });` On AbortError, return a 504 with `Retry-After: 5`. AbortController is available in CF Workers runtime.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low. Additive change in one file. Static fallback path in the client already handles non-ok responses.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Mock Groq to delay >10s; assert handleRoute returns 504 within ~11s.

mergedFindings.title: enriched_signals plain INSERT has no dedup key — duplicate rows created on cron drain retry after mid-flight crash
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/cron/src/drain.ts lines 212-220: processOne writes raw_dumps via idempotent UPSERT, then writes enriched_signals via plain INSERT with a new UUID. The drain.ts comment explicitly acknowledges: 'enriched_signals stays a plain INSERT: a duplicate there would need its own dedup key'. A crash between the two writes causes the retry to re-run the full Anthropic call and insert a second enriched_signals row with the same dump_id FK but a different UUID PK.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Downstream analytics (sector/brand/topic aggregations) double-count affected dumps. Each retry burns an additional Anthropic Haiku call (~$0.001). At scale or during queue backlog catch-up, this amplifies cost.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Data integrity gap. The code's own comment confirms the known gap. No dedup mechanism at the DB level.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add migration: `ALTER TABLE enriched_signals ADD CONSTRAINT enriched_signals_dump_id_unique UNIQUE (dump_id);` Then change the INSERT to use PostgREST header `Prefer: resolution=ignore-duplicates` (or `ON CONFLICT (dump_id) DO NOTHING`). The constraint doubles as protection against the queue double-processing scenario from Finding #2.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Requires a migration. If a future feature legitimately needs multiple enrichment rows per dump, the constraint must be lifted. Safe to accept for now.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: workers/cron/tests/drain.test.ts: call processOne twice for same dump id, assert enriched_signals INSERT is called twice but the second is a no-op (DB returns 409).

mergedFindings.title: Dual-auth identity mismatch: /enrich-dump uses Supabase JWT fallback while /route/dump uses Clerk-only — same user gets different telemetry hashes per session type
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/index.ts lines 344-371: /enrich-dump, /ingest-event, /label call verifyJwt() which returns either a Clerk sub (user_xxx) OR a Supabase UUID. /route/dump calls verifyClerkJwt() returning only Clerk sub. When the Supabase fallback fires, telemetry deriveUserHash receives a UUID; when Clerk fires it receives user_xxx. Same physical user gets different hashes depending on session age. Idempotency KV keys on /route/dump (dump:idem:${userId}:${dumpId}) never replay for Supabase-session users because the userId differs.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Analytics identity fragmentation: the same user appears as two identities in the telemetry corpus. Idempotency dedup breaks for transitional users who still have Supabase sessions.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Cross-session analytics are silently incorrect. Retry dedup is inert for affected users, potentially allowing duplicate AI calls.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Unify on Clerk auth across all endpoints now that CLERK_ISSUER is configured. Remove the Supabase fallback from verifyJwt() once Supabase sessions are confirmed expired, OR add a SUPABASE_SESSION_CUTOFF_EPOCH env var and reject Supabase tokens issued before that date.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Medium — removing Supabase fallback before all sessions have cycled breaks those users. Safe approach: add the cutoff epoch env var and reject pre-cutoff Supabase tokens gradually.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Assert that a Supabase JWT returns UUID-shaped userId and a Clerk JWT returns user_xxx, and that the telemetry hash differs — then fix by normalizing to one canonical form.

mergedFindings.title: /partner/pair endpoint allows brute-forcing 6-digit pairing codes at 100 req/min per authenticated user
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/index.ts line 118: PURCHASE_RATE_MAX = 100 req/min. Lines 229-243: all /partner/* routes use PURCHASE_RATE_MAX. workers/ai-proxy/src/router/partner.ts line 27: CODE_TTL_SEC = 1800s. Line 69: sixDigit() generates a 6-digit code (10^6 = 1M keyspace). At 100 req/min × 30 min TTL = 3,000 guesses per code window = 0.3% keyspace coverage per window. A targeted attack (partial code knowledge from shoulder-surfing) is practical.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Attacker can pair with a victim's account without consent and gain access to the partner's intimate-window snapshot: mood, crisis state, go-dark status. Highest severity if attacker has partial code knowledge.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Partner pairing auth relies solely on code secrecy, but the code space is small and the rate limit is designed for purchase bursts, not secret-code verification.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Lower /partner/pair rate limit to 5 req/min per user (not PURCHASE_RATE_MAX). Add a failed-attempt counter in KV: after 5 wrong guesses for one code, mark the code invalid and force re-generation on the minting side.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low. Localized to partner rate-limit constants in index.ts and partner.ts.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: POST /partner/pair with 6 wrong guesses → assert 429 or 410 is returned before exhausting the minute window.

mergedFindings.title: applyInbox drains dump_inbox with no page limit — O(N) blocking loop can exhaust CF Worker CPU budget for high-backlog users
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/router/server-apply.ts line 106: `rest(env, 'dump_inbox?user_id=eq.${userId}&status=eq.pending&select=*')` — no `&limit=` or `&order=` parameter. The `for (const row of rows)` loop decrypts and applies each row serially with 2 decrypt + 2 fetch calls per row. A user offline for an extended period could accumulate hundreds of pending rows. CF Worker CPU budget is 30s wall-clock.
mergedFindings.userImpact: First foreground sync after extended offline use can time out. Rows beyond the CF budget are never applied until the next /apply-inbox call, leaving the pantry in a partial state.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Worker CPU budget exhaustion for high-backlog users. Partial application with no indication to the client of how many rows remain.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add `&limit=50&order=created_at.asc` to the fetch URL. Return applied count in the response so clients know to poll /apply-inbox in a loop until applied < 50.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low — additive change to existing query.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Stub 200 pending rows; assert applyInbox applies ≤50 and returns accurate applied count.

mergedFindings.title: account-delete Clerk users cannot delete accounts — Supabase-only verifyJwtAndExtractUserId rejects Clerk JWTs
mergedFindings.evidence: apps/api/src/account-delete.ts lines 274-297: verifyJwtAndExtractUserId calls `GET /auth/v1/user` on the Supabase endpoint with the user's JWT. The Supabase /auth/v1/user endpoint only accepts Supabase-issued JWTs. Clerk-issued tokens (sub = user_xxx) are rejected with 401. Any user who signed up via Clerk and hits /account/delete gets a null userId and a 401 response from the handler, making account deletion impossible.
mergedFindings.userImpact: GDPR/App Store compliance blocker: Clerk-migrated users (likely the majority of current users) cannot delete their accounts through the official endpoint.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Account deletion broken for all post-Clerk-migration users. Silently returns 401 with no explanation.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add Clerk JWT verification as a first-try step in verifyJwtAndExtractUserId: try verifyClerkJwt first, extract sub if it resolves, fall back to Supabase /auth/v1/user for legacy sessions. Requires CLERK_ISSUER env var on the apps/api worker.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low — the dual-mode pattern is already proven in workers/ai-proxy/src/invites.ts.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: apps/api/tests/account-delete.test.ts: test with a Clerk-format JWT (user_xxx sub) and assert the handler resolves userId correctly.

mergedFindings.title: Brain-dump cron drain calls /v1/messages with 'x-user-id: cron-drain' — spoofable rate-limit bucket and shared with unauthenticated proxy
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/cron/src/drain.ts line 240: `'x-user-id': 'cron-drain'` is a fixed string sent to the AI_PROXY service binding. workers/ai-proxy/src/index.ts lines 443-445: /v1/messages uses that header as the rate-limit key with no JWT verification. Any public internet caller can also set `x-user-id: cron-drain` and share the cron's rate-limit bucket, effectively evicting the cron drain from its own quota. During a backlog (BATCH_CAP=50 per tick), 10 cron calls in 60s can hit the 10 req/min AI bucket for that literal key.
mergedFindings.userImpact: During heavy backlog catch-up, cron enrichment calls may be rate-limited, leaving KV entries for the next tick. An adversary spoofing 'x-user-id: cron-drain' amplifies budget drain from Finding #1.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Cron enrichment reliability degrades under backlog. Partially blocked by the fix for Finding #1 — once /v1/messages requires JWT, x-user-id spoofing becomes irrelevant.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Blocked by Finding #1 fix (add JWT to /v1/messages). After that fix, cron must switch to a pre-shared CRON_INTERNAL_SECRET header or call Anthropic directly (it already has ANTHROPIC_URL via env.AI_PROXY) bypassing the rate-limit entirely since it runs server-side.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low — cron runs in a service binding, not public internet. Direct Anthropic call is self-contained.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: workers/cron/tests/drain.test.ts: assert drainEnrichQueue with 50 items succeeds without hitting rate limit errors.

mergedFindings.title: Daily cron tasks (pattern detection, period prediction, subscription detection) are empty stubs — fire on active schedule but produce zero output
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/cron/src/index.ts lines 216-277: runPatternDetection, runPeriodPrediction, runSubscriptionDetection, runBodyWeeklyReview, runBodyCorrelations all have empty bodies with TODO comments. Lines 92-105: all five are called from the active 03:00 UTC cron trigger (wrangler.toml line 20). The stubs call no external services and return nothing.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Advertised intelligence layer (pattern detection, period prediction, subscription detection) produces zero server-side output. Alpha users and co-founders evaluating the product see no server-side insights despite them being listed in roadmap docs.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Active cron trigger runs 5 no-op functions daily at 03:00 UTC. If any stub accidentally starts doing something in the future it will be undetected.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Product decision: (a) remove the 03:00 UTC cron trigger until stubs are real, and document in CHECKLIST.md that these are client-side only for now, OR (b) fast-path port packages/logic/patterns to the worker for at least one signal. At minimum add a structured log line per stub so alerting can detect unexpected behavior.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: None for removing the trigger. Stubs are already no-ops.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Integration test that cron stubs emit a structured log line when they run, so monitoring catches if they start producing side effects.

mergedFindings.title: validate-invite/generate-invite — upstreamError strips errText from client (not a leak), but status code is echoed in some error paths
mergedFindings.evidence: packages/worker-http/src/index.ts lines 44-63: upstreamError() logs `detail` server-side only and returns `json({ error: code, request_id: requestId }, status)` to the client — errText is NOT forwarded. Round 3 suspected this as a leak but the code confirms it is already handled. The residual risk: the upstream HTTP status code is passed as the second arg to upstreamError and echoed in the Response status (e.g., 502 for Supabase 409), which reveals that a 409 from Supabase occurred — but no column names or schema details leak.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Minimal. An attacker learns the upstream returned a conflict (409→502) but no DB schema details are exposed.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Not a real vulnerability. Echoing upstream status in the wrapper response status (502) is standard practice. No fix required unless strict information-hiding is desired.
mergedFindings.dissent: Round 3 flagged this as a suspected leak needing verification. Direct code read of packages/worker-http/src/index.ts confirms the errText is stripped before the client response is constructed. Downgraded from P3 suspected to P4 confirmed-non-issue.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: No fix required. Already handled by upstreamError. Optionally normalize all upstream error responses to a fixed 502 regardless of upstream status code for strict information hiding.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: None.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Existing test: confirm a 409 from Supabase on /generate-invite returns a client body containing only { error, request_id } with no PostgREST field names.

implementationRuntimeMismatches: Finding #2 (wrangler.toml queue bindings): comment says 'intentionally left commented' but the TOML block is uncommented and active. Cannot determine from static analysis whether the queue is provisioned in CF — runtime check (`wrangler queues list`) required to pick the correct fix branch.

Finding #3 (cacheHitUpdate hit_count): route.test.ts mocks the PATCH to 204 without validating the body — the test passes while the production call silently fails with a 400 type error on every cache hit. Implementation says 'increment' but runtime PostgREST ignores it.

Finding #13 (upstreamError errText leak): Round 3 suspected a client-facing leak. Direct code read of packages/worker-http/src/index.ts confirms errText is logged server-side only and stripped from client responses. Round 3 dissent resolved: this is NOT a live vulnerability.
topRisks: /brain-dump + /v1/messages have zero auth — ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is effectively public to anyone who finds the worker URL. Financial liability and service disruption with no audit trail.
wrangler.toml queue binding TOML/comment mismatch — either CI deploy is permanently broken OR enrichment double-processes every dump. Cannot determine which without runtime check.
account-delete Clerk users get 401 (Supabase-only JWT check rejects Clerk tokens) — GDPR/App Store compliance blocker for the entire post-migration user base.

/partner/pair code brute-force: 6-digit code at 100 req/min rate limit (designed for purchase bursts) allows ~3000 guesses per 30-min code TTL — stalker/adversary can pair without consent and access mood+crisis data.
quickWins: Add verifyClerkJwt guard to /brain-dump and /v1/messages (6 lines, mirrors /route/dump pattern already in the same file) — closes the open Anthropic proxy immediately.
Run `wrangler queues list` to determine queue provisioning state, then either fix the comment or comment out the TOML block — 1-line fix + 1-line comment change, prevents CI breakage.

Replace `{ hit_count: { increment: 1 } }` with a PostgREST RPC call in route.ts AND feed-me.ts — 1 migration + 2-line TS change, restores cache analytics that have been dead since the feature shipped.
Add `checkRate(..., 20)` for /validate-invite and /claim-invite (5 lines each, existing checkRate infra available) — closes invite enumeration with no migration required.
Lower /partner/pair rate limit to 5 req/min and add a 5-attempt lockout in KV — prevents intimate-data exposure with a 2-line constant change + ~20 lines of KV counter logic.

angleSummary: The database layer has three clusters of critical problems: (1) GDPR/account-delete is mechanically broken — the JWT verifier calls a Supabase Auth endpoint that rejects Clerk JWTs, so every deletion attempt returns 401, and even if fixed, 5 Clerk-user-scoped tables are absent from the cascade list; (2) the identity model is split — profiles still carries a uuid FK to auth.users and all its RLS policies use auth.uid() which returns NULL under Clerk, making the table inert for all current users and breaking cross-device salt roaming silently; (3) multiple schema-level defects (dead RLS policies, missing CHECK constraint value, no tombstone purge, no unpair cleanup, LWW timestamp manipulation vector) compound these core problems.

mergedFindings.title: account-delete JWT verifier calls Supabase /auth/v1/user — always 401 for Clerk users, GDPR deletion completely non-functional
mergedFindings.evidence: apps/api/src/account-delete.ts line 279: verifyJwtAndExtractUserId calls GET /auth/v1/user with the Bearer token. Supabase Auth rejects Clerk JWTs (different issuer/secret). apps/api/tests/account-delete.test.ts mocks the /auth/v1/user response so tests pass and hide the live breakage. Round 3 only — Rounds 1 and 2 inspected account-delete but focused on the table-list gap rather than the JWT verifier itself.
mergedFindings.dissent: Rounds 1 and 2 did not flag the JWT verifier breakage; they treated account-delete as partially functional. Round 3 is the only round that traced the actual HTTP call. The finding is mechanically certain (Supabase /auth/v1/user cannot verify a Clerk-issued JWT) but was missed by two rounds, hence confidence 1. Severity elevated to P0 because this means the App Store account-deletion requirement (APSL §5.1.1) and GDPR Art. 17 have never been satisfied.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Every user who attempts to delete their account gets a silent failure. This is a legal requirement (GDPR, CCPA) and an App Store mandatory feature. The entire account-delete flow is dead in production.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Replace verifyJwtAndExtractUserId with the Clerk JWT verifier already in workers/ai-proxy/src/clerk-verify.ts. Extract sub from the verified JWT as the Clerk user ID. The deleteAuthUser step must be changed to call the Clerk user-delete API instead of Supabase, since Supabase has no Clerk user row to delete.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Medium. JWT verifier swap is straightforward. Must also ensure all USER_SCOPED_TABLES filters use the Clerk text ID (not a Supabase UUID), and the deleteAuthUser step must not call Supabase Auth for a user that was never created there.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Integration test: pass a real Clerk-shaped JWT (sub = 'user_XXX'), assert verifier accepts it, assert cascade DELETEs fire for the correct Clerk user ID.

mergedFindings.title: GDPR cascade misses 5 Clerk-user-scoped tables: dump_inbox, grocery_pantry, partner_codes, partner_pairs, partner_snapshots
mergedFindings.evidence: apps/api/src/account-delete.ts USER_SCOPED_TABLES (lines 111-125) lists only: encrypted_state, finance_records, plaid_inbox, plaid_items, scheduled_jobs, push_tokens, profiles. Missing: dump_inbox and grocery_pantry (supabase/migrations/20260611000001_server_apply_a6b.sql, user_id text, no auth.users FK); partner_codes, partner_pairs, partner_snapshots (20260602103016_partner_bilateral_sync.sql, all Clerk text user_id, no auth.users FK). All five were dropped from the Postgres cascade safety net in 20260618000002. Round 1 did not flag these specific tables.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Deleted accounts permanently retain queued brain-dump fragments (dump_inbox), server-side grocery pantry data (grocery_pantry), partner pairing codes/pairs (partner_codes/partner_pairs), and partner intimate-window snapshots (crisis flag, mood phrases, gone_dark) in partner_snapshots. GDPR Art. 17 violation. App Store review risk.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add to USER_SCOPED_TABLES in account-delete.ts: {table:'dump_inbox',column:'user_id'}, {table:'grocery_pantry',column:'user_id'}, {table:'partner_codes',column:'user_id'}, {table:'partner_snapshots',column:'user_id'}. For partner_pairs: two DELETEs — WHERE user_lo = userId and WHERE user_hi = userId — since the user can appear in either column.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low for four of the five. Medium for partner_pairs (dual-column match, cannot use the standard single-column filter loop).
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Seed all five tables in the account-delete integration test; assert zero rows for the deleted user across all five tables post-delete.

mergedFindings.title: profiles table dead for all Clerk users: uuid FK to auth.users + auth.uid() RLS policies always NULL under Clerk JWT — salt roaming silently broken
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260512000002_profiles.sql line 32: id uuid PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES auth.users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE. Lines 107-126: all four RLS policies use auth.uid() = id. supabase/migrations/20260618000002_identity_clerk_text.sql lines 236-241: 'DELIBERATELY NOT touched here'. Under Clerk JWT, auth.uid() returns NULL — RLS policies always deny. packages/auth/src/index.ts confirms auth package no longer writes to profiles. account-delete.ts line 125 DELETEs profiles by UUID which matches 0 rows for any Clerk user. profile_recovery_lookup RPC returns 0 rows for all Clerk users, making cross-device salt roaming non-functional.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Cross-device encryption key recovery (salt roaming) is silently broken for every Clerk user. Users who lose their device cannot recover encrypted data. The profiles DELETE in the GDPR flow is a no-op. Any code that tries to use profile_recovery_lookup will silently fail.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Product decision required: (a) Formally deprecate and DROP profiles + profile_recovery_lookup (salt lives on device only, roaming is removed as a feature) — lower risk; or (b) Migrate profiles.id to text Clerk ID, drop FK to auth.users, rekey all RLS to auth.jwt()->>''sub'', wire a profiles UPSERT in the Clerk post-sign-in path — restores roaming but significant migration effort.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low for option (a) if table is confirmed empty. Medium for option (b): FK drop + type migration + RLS rewrite + new write path.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Confirm profile_recovery_lookup returns 0 rows for a Clerk user (demonstrates breakage). After fix: either assert table is dropped or assert a Clerk sign-in creates a profiles row and a second-device sign-in recovers the salt.

mergedFindings.title: partner_snapshots not deleted on unpair — intimate-window data (crisis, mood phrases, gone_dark) persists after couple breaks up
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/router/partner.ts unpair() (line 200-203): calls only dropPairsFor() which DELETEs from partner_pairs. No code anywhere deletes from partner_snapshots on unpair. grep for 'partner_snapshots.*delete' and 'DELETE.*partner_snapshots' across workers/ returns no hits. Round 1 did not flag this specific issue.
mergedFindings.userImpact: After unpairing, intimate-window data (crisis flag, mood/energy phrases, gone_dark) persists indefinitely on the server for the ex-user. This is sensitive personal health data that the user reasonably expects to be erased when a partnership ends.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: In partner.ts unpair(): after dropPairsFor(), add DELETE to partner_snapshots WHERE user_id = me. Same service_role pattern as other partner table cleanup in the same file.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low. Two-line addition to an existing function.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Integration test: pair two users, unpair, assert partner_snapshots row for the calling user is deleted.

mergedFindings.title: grocery_purchase_history self-select RLS policy uses auth.uid()::text — always NULL/false under Clerk JWT, policy is permanently dead
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260615000001_grocery_purchase_history_user_id_text.sql lines 27-30: USING (auth.uid()::text = user_id). Under Clerk JWT, auth.uid() returns NULL; NULL::text = user_id evaluates to NULL (falsy under RLS). Migration 20260618000002 converted other tables to auth.jwt()->>''sub'' but explicitly skipped grocery_purchase_history (line 15: 'already retyped'). The GRANT to authenticated exists but the RLS check always denies. Workers read via service_role (bypassing RLS) so /replenishment/:user endpoint is unaffected today.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Any future client-side direct query against grocery_purchase_history silently returns 0 rows. Current user-facing impact is low since the only read path is via the worker's service_role connection. Latent correctness bug.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: New migration: DROP POLICY grocery_purchase_history_self_select ON public.grocery_purchase_history; CREATE POLICY grocery_purchase_history_self_select ON public.grocery_purchase_history FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (auth.jwt() ->> 'sub' = user_id);
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Very low — policy currently always denies; replacing it adds access that was always intended.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Integration test: authenticated Clerk user reads their own grocery_purchase_history rows via direct Supabase REST (not service_role).

mergedFindings.title: routing_cache module CHECK constraint missing 'medication' — cache writes for medication module silently fail, cache permanently cold
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260521000001_routing_cache.sql lines 30-33: CHECK constraint lists 13 modules, 'medication' absent. workers/ai-proxy/src/router/route.ts lines 118-130: MODULE_CONFIGS includes 'medication' as a routable module. cacheWrite() fires on cache miss (line 341) but the INSERT is rejected by the CHECK constraint. The error is swallowed by a console.error only (line 342). Rounds 1 and 2 did not inspect route.ts against the CHECK constraint.
mergedFindings.dissent: Only Round 3 caught this. The finding is mechanically certain (the value is absent from the SQL CHECK constraint, and route.ts includes it as a valid module). Confidence 1 because Rounds 1 and 2 missed it, but the static evidence is unambiguous.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Every medication module AI routing call pays full Voyage + Groq cost with no cache benefit. Silent, no error surfaced to users. Ongoing cost drain.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: New migration: ALTER TABLE public.routing_cache DROP CONSTRAINT routing_cache_module_check; ALTER TABLE public.routing_cache ADD CONSTRAINT routing_cache_module_check CHECK (module IN ('grocery','work','body','dump','money','admin','pets','habits','health','finance','sleep','cycle','goals','medication'));
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Very low. Adding a value to a CHECK constraint is non-destructive and non-blocking.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Worker integration test: medication routing cache miss triggers a DB INSERT without constraint violation.

mergedFindings.title: LWW updated_at trigger allows client to supply far-future timestamp and permanently win conflict resolution on encrypted_state and finance_records
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260512000001_encrypted_state.sql line 70 and supabase/migrations/20260514000008_finance_records.sql line 103: triggers clamp timestamps only below now() — if new.updated_at < now() then set to now(). Values above now() pass through unchanged. A client supplying updated_at = '2999-01-01' will permanently win LWW on that row against all future device writes. Rounds 2 and 3 did not inspect these triggers.
mergedFindings.dissent: Only Round 1 caught this. Confidence 1, but the trigger SQL is unambiguous: the upper-bound clamp is absent.
mergedFindings.userImpact: A buggy or compromised client can lock an encrypted module state or finance record so no future device can ever overwrite it. Silent data corruption that is difficult to diagnose.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Change both triggers: if new.updated_at is null or new.updated_at < now() or new.updated_at > now() + interval '5 seconds' then new.updated_at := now(); end if; — allows small clock skew, rejects far-future values.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low — additive condition, no data loss, trivially reversible.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: SQL test: INSERT row with updated_at = now() + interval '1 year'; assert resulting updated_at is approximately now().

mergedFindings.title: HNSW vector index on routing_cache.embedding is not module-partitioned — ANN search bleeds across module boundaries
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260521000001_routing_cache.sql lines 59-62: single HNSW index over ALL rows. supabase/migrations/20260618000003_routing_cache_revive.sql lines 77-83: lookup function adds WHERE module = $1 AFTER the vector similarity expression. pgvector HNSW does not support WHERE-clause partitioned indexes; the ANN scan traverses all 13 module embeddings before post-filter. The routing_cache comment (line 27) explicitly states 'Always filter on this — module boundaries must not bleed.' The index design violates this invariant. Rounds 1 and 3 did not inspect this.
mergedFindings.dissent: Only Round 2 caught this. Confidence 1, but the pgvector behavior is well-documented: HNSW with post-filter can return cross-module results when the nearest geometric neighbor belongs to a different module.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Wrong-module cache hits cause misrouted brain dump classification. A grocery query could return a cached 'work' classification. Silent and insidious — no error, just wrong behavior.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Create 13 partial HNSW indexes, one per module: CREATE INDEX routing_cache_hnsw_grocery ON routing_cache USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WHERE module = 'grocery'; — repeat for each module. Drop the global index after verifying partial indexes are used.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Medium — HNSW index builds on large tables are slow; must be done during low-traffic window with CONCURRENTLY option where supported.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Test that routing_cache_lookup with p_module='grocery' never returns a row whose stored module column is not 'grocery'.

mergedFindings.title: GDPR telemetry erasure gap: user_hash-keyed tables (raw_dumps, enriched_signals, consent_audit) cannot be deleted if hash is deterministic from Clerk ID
mergedFindings.evidence: apps/api/src/account-delete.ts lines 49-53 (comment): anonymized rows carry user_hash, not user_id. supabase/migrations/20260514000001_raw_dumps.sql line 15: user_hash is the only identity column. No hash→clerk_id reverse mapping exists. If user_hash = sha256(clerk_id), the hash is non-reversible but the rows are still linkable by a data authority given the Clerk ID. Rounds 2 and 3 explicitly noted these tables should NOT receive cascade deletes (the anonymized design is intentional) but Round 1 correctly identified the regulatory gap.
mergedFindings.dissent: Round 3 explicitly said 'do not add user_id columns or cascade deletes to them' — intentionally anonymized. Round 1 treats this as a potential GDPR violation. Both are correct simultaneously: the tables are intentionally anonymous but the legal argument depends on the hash function. If HMAC with a per-user secret, key deletion = effective erasure (GDPR-safe). If bare sha256, a data authority can argue the rows are pseudonymous, not anonymous. This is a product/legal decision, not a pure code fix.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Regulatory risk (GDPR Art. 17) if hash is a bare sha256(clerk_id). At minimum, the hash function must be documented and reviewed by counsel. At most, a salted HMAC scheme where the salt can be deleted per-user is needed.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Verify and document the hash function used in workers. If bare sha256: migrate to HMAC(clerk_id, per-user-secret) where the secret is stored in a secrets table that IS included in the GDPR cascade. If already HMAC with server secret: document that secret rotation/deletion at account-delete time constitutes effective erasure and add that step to account-delete.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: High if changing hash scheme (backfill migration + all workers that compute user_hash). Low if the hash is already HMAC and the documentation/deletion of the secret is the only missing step.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: After account deletion, verify the hash key cannot be reconstructed (secret deleted or rotated to an irrecoverable value).

mergedFindings.title: partner_codes expired rows accumulate indefinitely — no server-side TTL cleanup
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260602103016_partner_bilateral_sync.sql line 18: expires_at timestamptz NOT NULL, no index on expires_at. workers/cron/src/index.ts: no cleanup task for partner_codes. workers/ai-proxy/src/router/partner.ts line 90: mintCode() deletes only the minting user's prior code — stale codes from churned/inactive users accumulate. Expiry checked application-side only (line 119).
mergedFindings.userImpact: Table grows unbounded. At scale, stale codes add noise. 6-digit code space makes collisions increasingly likely over time (birthday paradox at ~2,000 live rows). Low immediate impact.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add one line to the daily cron task in workers/cron/src/index.ts: DELETE FROM partner_codes WHERE expires_at < now(). Optionally add a migration with an index on expires_at for efficient filtering.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Very low.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Cron unit test asserting expired partner_codes rows are purged; assert valid unexpired codes are retained.

mergedFindings.title: finance_records soft-delete tombstones accumulate indefinitely — no purge schedule, no partial index
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260514000008_finance_records.sql line 65: deleted_at timestamptz nullable soft-delete marker. Lines 81-89: two indexes on (user_id, updated_at) — no partial index excluding deleted rows. packages/sync/src/finance.ts lines 371, 516-519: tombstones are upserted on delete. grep for 'purge', 'vacuum', 'deleted_at.*interval' across all migrations and workers returns no hits. Round 3 did not flag this independently.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Delta-sync cursor queries (WHERE updated_at > last_cursor) re-download and re-process tombstones on every device sync. Long-lived users with many finance mutations accumulate unbounded tombstone rows. Negligible at alpha scale; latency issue at production scale.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add partial index: CREATE INDEX finance_records_live_user_idx ON finance_records (user_id, updated_at DESC) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL. Add daily cron sweep: DELETE FROM finance_records WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL AND deleted_at < now() - interval '30 days'.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low for index (additive). Medium for DELETE sweep (requires all devices to have synced within 30 days; no device last-seen table currently exists to enforce this).
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Assert delta-sync with partial-index hint does not return deleted_at IS NOT NULL rows. Integration test: tombstone row older than 30 days is purged by cron.

mergedFindings.title: module_events.session_id has no FK to session_events — orphan rows accumulate silently
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260514000005_module_events.sql: session_id uuid NOT NULL, no REFERENCES session_events(session_id). supabase/migrations/20260514000004_session_events.sql: session_id is UNIQUE. No ON DELETE CASCADE. If a session_events row is absent or deleted, corresponding module_events rows become orphans with no parent context. Rounds 2 and 3 did not flag this.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Data integrity: analytics joins on user_hash + session_id can produce phantom module-open counts from sessions that never officially started or ended. No user-facing impact today but corrupts future cohort analysis.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Migration: ALTER TABLE public.module_events ADD CONSTRAINT module_events_session_fk FOREIGN KEY (session_id) REFERENCES public.session_events(session_id) ON DELETE CASCADE; First clean orphan rows: DELETE FROM module_events me WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM session_events se WHERE se.session_id = me.session_id);
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Medium — if orphan rows already exist in prod, the ALTER will fail. Must count orphans first.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Assert INSERT into module_events with a non-existent session_id is rejected by the FK constraint.

mergedFindings.title: 17 migrations (20260521 onward) have no rollback files — emergency rollback for identity rewrite and partner schema is manual/undocumented
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/rollbacks/ contains 20 files covering only 20260512–20260519. The 17 migrations from 20260521000001 onward — including 20260618000002 (identity rewrite across 6 tables), 20260618000003 (routing_cache RPC + column), 20260611000001 (server_apply tables), 20260602103016 (partner schema) — have no .down.sql counterpart. Rounds 1 and 2 did not flag this.
mergedFindings.userImpact: If a bad migration reaches prod, there is no tested rollback path for the most consequential schema changes. Rollback under incident pressure requires manually crafting reversal SQL.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: None — rollback files are applied manually only when needed.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: None. Operational discipline item.

mergedFindings.title: partner_snapshots missing updated_at trigger — stale timestamps possible if caller omits field in future UPDATE
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260602103016_partner_bilateral_sync.sql line 44: updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now() — default only fires on INSERT, no before-update trigger. partner.ts line 189: putSnapshot manually sets updated_at in the upsert payload today. All other timestamp-bearing tables in the schema have a server-side trigger (encrypted_state_touch, profiles_touch, push_tokens_touch). Rounds 1 and 2 did not flag this.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Invisible today. If any future code path issues an UPDATE without including updated_at, the timestamp stays stale — partner's client reads old mood/crisis state believing it is current.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add a before-update trigger on partner_snapshots matching the pattern of other tables: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION partner_snapshots_touch() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at := now(); RETURN NEW; END; $$; CREATE TRIGGER partner_snapshots_touch BEFORE UPDATE ON partner_snapshots FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE PROCEDURE partner_snapshots_touch();
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Very low.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: SQL test: UPDATE partner_snapshots without setting updated_at; assert updated_at advances.

mergedFindings.title: replenishment.ts file-level comment says uuid but function signature is now text — stale developer documentation
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/router/replenishment.ts line 5: comment reads 'grocery_replenishment_estimates(uuid)'. After supabase/migrations/20260615000001, the actual function signature is grocery_replenishment_estimates(p_user text). Code is functionally correct; comment is stale.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Developer confusion only. No runtime impact.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Change line 5: 'grocery_replenishment_estimates(uuid)' → 'grocery_replenishment_estimates(text)'.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: None.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: None required.

implementationRuntimeMismatches: account-delete.ts JWT verifier (calls Supabase /auth/v1/user) vs. Clerk-issued JWTs in production: tests pass (mocked) but live calls return 401 — complete runtime breakage masked by mock
profiles RLS policies use auth.uid() which is NULL under Clerk JWT: schema appears functional in static review but is permanently denied at runtime for all Clerk users
grocery_purchase_history self-select RLS: policy text looks plausible (auth.uid()::text = user_id) but evaluates to NULL/false at runtime because Clerk JWT does not populate auth.uid()
routing_cache HNSW index: schema review shows an index exists, but at runtime pgvector ANN search does not respect the post-filter WHERE module = $1, enabling cross-module cache hits
routing_cache CHECK constraint vs MODULE_CONFIGS in route.ts: 'medication' is a valid routable module in TypeScript but is absent from the SQL constraint, causing silent INSERT failures at runtime
topRisks: account-delete is legally broken (GDPR Art. 17, CCPA, App Store APSL §5.1.1): Clerk JWTs are rejected by the Supabase Auth verifier — every deletion attempt silently returns 401 in production

5 Clerk-user-scoped tables (dump_inbox, grocery_pantry, partner_codes, partner_pairs, partner_snapshots) have no auth.users FK cascade and are absent from the GDPR deletion cascade — intimate partner data persists indefinitely after account deletion

profiles identity model is irreconcilably split: uuid FK to auth.users + auth.uid() RLS policies are permanently dead under Clerk JWT — cross-device salt roaming (encryption key recovery) is silently broken for every user
quickWins: Fix grocery_purchase_history self-select policy: one migration, replace auth.uid()::text with auth.jwt() ->> 'sub' (< 10 min, zero risk)

Add 5 missing tables to account-delete.ts USER_SCOPED_TABLES: dump_inbox, grocery_pantry, partner_codes, partner_snapshots + two-pass partner_pairs (< 30 min, no schema change, enables GDPR completeness once JWT verifier is also fixed)
Add DELETE partner_snapshots in partner.ts unpair() after dropPairsFor() (2 lines, zero risk)
Add DELETE FROM partner_codes WHERE expires_at < now() to daily cron task (1 line)
Add 'medication' to routing_cache module CHECK constraint (1 migration, restores cache cost savings for medication module)
Fix replenishment.ts line 5 comment: uuid → text (1-line non-functional change)

angleSummary: The auth layer has two P0/P1 compliance failures and a cluster of P2 defense-in-depth gaps. The most critical: account-delete.ts uses Supabase-only JWT verification but all current users authenticate via Clerk, meaning every real delete request returns 401 and user data is never actually erased — a clear GDPR/App Store violation. The /brain-dump and /v1/messages endpoints are unauthenticated Anthropic proxies that anyone can hit to drain the API key. Rate-limit enforcement is broken on multiple paths (null-skip, spoofable x-user-id header, missing bindings on invite endpoints). A legacy Supabase auth fallback has no sunset mechanism. Clerk JWT verification omits the audience claim. A draft security-invoker migration for invite_funnel views was written but never applied to prod.

mergedFindings.title: account-delete silently fails for all Clerk users — GDPR erasure and App Store delete-account requirement broken
mergedFindings.evidence: apps/api/src/account-delete.ts lines 274–296: verifyJwtAndExtractUserId() calls GET /auth/v1/user with the bearer token, which returns 401 for Clerk JWTs (no Supabase Auth user backs them). Round 2 further confirmed that even if the JWT were accepted, deleteUserRows() builds WHERE user_id = eq.<supabase-uuid> but Clerk-era tables (encrypted_state, finance_records, scheduled_jobs, push_tokens, plaid_inbox, plaid_items, partner_snapshots, dump_inbox, cook_history, grocery_pantry, partner_codes, partner_pairs, grocery_purchase_history) all store user_id as a Clerk text sub ('user_2abc…') after migration 20260618000002. Round 3 confirmed the dual-mode verifyJwt from invites.ts is NOT imported in this handler.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Every current user who taps 'Delete My Account' gets a silent 401. The auth.users row may or may not be deleted (service-role step) but all personal data rows are orphaned. GDPR Art. 17 and CCPA erasure rights are violated. App Store guideline 5.1.1 requires a working in-app deletion flow — this breaks it.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Two compounding bugs: (1) JWT verify always fails for Clerk users → 401 before any data deletion. (2) Even if fixed, the wrong user ID type is used, so 0 rows would be deleted from 13 tables. auth.users deletion may or may not succeed depending on whether it uses service-role independently. Orphaned data in partner_snapshots (crisis flag, mood phrases) is particularly sensitive.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Replace verifyJwtAndExtractUserId() with the dual-mode verifyJwt() from invites.ts. Add all post-Clerk tables to USER_SCOPED_TABLES: grocery_purchase_history, cook_history, dump_inbox, grocery_pantry, partner_codes, partner_pairs, partner_snapshots. partner_pairs needs a 2-column OR delete (user_lo / user_hi). Add Clerk user deletion via Clerk Backend API (requires CLERK_SECRET_KEY as a new secret in apps/api).
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Medium — touches account deletion; needs integration test with a real Clerk JWT mock. The Clerk user deletion step requires a new API call not currently wired.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: apps/api/tests/account-delete.test.ts: test that a Clerk-shaped JWT mock results in ok:true and deleteUserRows called with the Clerk sub. Test that all 13 tables are included in deletion. Existing Supabase-JWT tests should remain passing.
mergedFindings.dissent: Round 1 raised this as P1 (two compounding bugs discovered sequentially). Round 3 escalated to P0 noting that the first bug (JWT verify 401) means deletion never even begins for any live user. Merged at P0 because the broken GDPR erasure path applies to 100% of current users with no workaround.

mergedFindings.title: /brain-dump and /v1/messages are unauthenticated Anthropic proxy endpoints — anyone can drain ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/index.ts lines 436–508: no JWT check in the handler block for /brain-dump or /v1/messages. Rate-limit key is req.headers.get('x-user-id') || req.headers.get('cf-connecting-ip') || 'anon' (lines 442–445). The 'anon' bucket is shared across all headerless callers. CORS is browser-only and irrelevant to curl/scripts. Round 2 confirmed BrainDumpInput.tsx calls routeDump → /route/dump only, suggesting the endpoint is dead on the active client. Round 3 flagged packages/api/src/anthropic.ts line 140 still references /brain-dump.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Any external actor with the *.workers.dev URL can POST arbitrary prompts billed to Ollie's Anthropic key. A bot rotating x-user-id values bypasses per-user rate-limit. The shared 'anon' bucket means one headerless bot exhausts it and DoS-es all other unauthenticated callers simultaneously.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Unlimited Anthropic API cost amplification. Service-level bill shock or quota exhaustion blocks all Ollie AI features. The 5-min KV cache only helps for identical bodies.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Confirm packages/api/src/anthropic.ts and any other caller no longer use /brain-dump. If confirmed dead, delete the endpoint entirely (2 lines removed). If not, wrap it in the same Clerk JWT guard as /route/dump (dump.ts lines 148–165). Remove or 401 /v1/messages as it is a legacy alias.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low if endpoint is deleted. If other callers exist outside the repo they break — grep routeViaHaiku call sites first.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Test that POST /brain-dump without Authorization returns 401. Test that POST /brain-dump with an invalid JWT returns 401.

mergedFindings.title: /validate-invite and /claim-invite have no app-level rate limiting despite wrangler.toml having no CF rate-limit binding for these paths
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/index.ts lines 376–381: both routes dispatch to handlers with zero rate-limit check. workers/ai-proxy/src/invites.ts lines 20–21: comment says 'rely on per-IP CF rate limit' but workers/ai-proxy/wrangler.toml has no [[ratelimits]] binding covering these paths — only TELEM_RATE_LIMITER and AI_RATE_LIMITER are bound. validate-invite is fully unauthenticated; claim-invite is authenticated but also unrate-limited. Round 1 noted the same: 'Validate and claim are not user-rate-limited but rely on the per-IP CF rate limit' comment is false.
mergedFindings.userImpact: An attacker can enumerate invite codes at full Cloudflare edge throughput. The format 'olli-XXXX-YYYY' from a 32-char alphabet (4-char segments) means 30^8 ≈ 656B theoretical keyspace, but with 30-day TTL and a small pool of active codes the practical enumeration window is much smaller. Invite system integrity compromised.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Invite code enumeration via /validate-invite. Supabase SELECT hits on every call with service-role key. At scale burns Supabase REST quota.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add a checkRate() call before handleValidateInvite and handleClaimInvite in index.ts using env.TELEM_RATE_LIMITER keyed on cf-connecting-ip. Cap at 20 req/min for validate, 5 req/min for claim. The existing checkRate() helper takes 4 lines to wire.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Negligible — additive rate-limit check.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: workers/ai-proxy/tests/invites.test.ts: test that the 21st validate-invite call from the same IP in a minute gets 429. Same for claim-invite at 6th call.
mergedFindings.dissent: Round 1 reported this as P2. Rounds 2 and 3 confirmed the missing wrangler.toml binding making the comment about 'CF rate limit' factually wrong, elevating confidence and practical severity to P1.

mergedFindings.title: resolveUserIdForRateLimit trusts spoofable x-user-id header as rate-limit key — attacker can DoS victim's API quota or skip rate limiting entirely
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/index.ts lines 520–535: resolveUserIdForRateLimit falls back to req.headers.get('x-user-id') after JWT verify. The rate-limit check fires BEFORE the auth check in index.ts (confirmed by Round 3). Two attack vectors: (1) attacker sets x-user-id=victim_clerk_id → burns victim's rate-limit bucket while attacker's real identity is not logged; (2) attacker omits all headers entirely → function returns null → caller uses `if (purchaseUserId) { checkRate(...) }` guard → rate limit is skipped entirely. Affects /grocery/purchase, /cook-history, /transcribe, /partner/*, /feed-me.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Vector 1: targeted DoS — authenticated user's quota drained before their own requests arrive. Vector 2: unlimited calls to /grocery/purchase etc with no rate limit, corrupting the replenishment model or triggering downstream AI cost.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Rate-limit key pollution and null-skip bypass. The auth check still rejects unauthenticated calls, but the rate-limit tick has already been consumed (vector 1) or skipped (vector 2).
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Two changes: (1) Remove x-user-id from the fallback chain in resolveUserIdForRateLimit — use only verified JWT sub or cf-connecting-ip. (2) Change final return from null to cf-connecting-ip || 'anon' and remove the `if (purchaseUserId)` guard in callers so rate-limit always runs.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low — affects rate-limit key selection only; no auth logic change.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Test that a request with x-user-id but no valid JWT keys the rate-limit on IP not x-user-id. Test that a request with no headers still hits the rate-limit check (not skipped).

mergedFindings.title: account-delete USER_SCOPED_TABLES missing 7 post-Clerk tables — sensitive data never deleted even after ID fix
mergedFindings.evidence: apps/api/src/account-delete.ts lines 111–126 (USER_SCOPED_TABLES): lists only encrypted_state, finance_records, plaid_inbox, plaid_items, scheduled_jobs, push_tokens, profiles. Missing: grocery_purchase_history (migration 20260522000001), cook_history (20260522000002), dump_inbox (20260611000001), grocery_pantry, partner_codes, partner_pairs, partner_snapshots (20260602103016). partner_snapshots stores crisis boolean and mood phrases — among the most sensitive data in the app.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Even after the Clerk-ID fix is applied, a user's grocery history, cook history, brain-dump inbox fragments, pantry state, and partner emotional snapshots are never erased. GDPR/CCPA data minimization breach on intimate-window data.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Structural incompleteness — the table list was last updated before the Clerk-era migration wave. partner_pairs uses user_lo/user_hi columns and needs a custom 2-column OR delete rather than a simple WHERE user_id=.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add all 7 tables to USER_SCOPED_TABLES. Implement a custom deletePartnerPairs() for the user_lo/user_hi composite. Tie this to finding #1 fix — same PR.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low. Service-role deletes are idempotent.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Unit test: USER_SCOPED_TABLES exactly matches all tables with a user_id column derived from current migrations. Test partner_pairs deletion covers both user_lo and user_hi rows.

mergedFindings.title: Legacy Supabase auth fallback in verifyJwt() has no expiry mechanism — indefinite dual-auth bridge
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/invites.ts lines 379–415: verifyJwt() tries Clerk first; if Clerk returns null it falls through to Supabase /auth/v1/user round-trip. Comment says 'removed once Supabase sessions fully aged out' but there is no flag, no cutoff date, no alerting when the Supabase path is taken. As long as SUPABASE_ANON_KEY is in the env the fallback is live. This applies to /generate-invite, /claim-invite, /enrich-dump, /ingest-event, and /label. The Supabase path returns a UUID while Clerk returns 'user_xxx' — mixing in DB analytics.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Any valid (or forged) legacy Supabase JWT authenticates to invite generation and telemetry writes indefinitely. An expired Clerk token that fails Clerk verify will also cause an extra Supabase round-trip (~200–300ms latency penalty) before also failing there.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Two credential rotation requirements. A stolen long-lived Supabase JWT grants access on these endpoints even after Clerk is fully deployed. No automatic enforcement of cutover.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add a SUPABASE_FALLBACK_ENABLED env flag (default '0'). Skip Supabase path unless explicitly '1'. Alternatively add SUPABASE_FALLBACK_CUTOFF_DATE — after that date, skip the path and log an error if it would have been taken. Coordinate cutover with confirmation that all Supabase sessions have expired.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Medium operationally — if any active users still hold Supabase-only sessions they would be logged out. Coordinate with a session-expiry audit first.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Test that a Supabase JWT is rejected when SUPABASE_FALLBACK_ENABLED is '0'. Test that it is accepted when '1'. Test that when SUPABASE_FALLBACK_CUTOFF_DATE is in the past the Supabase path is skipped.

mergedFindings.title: invite_funnel views are security_definer (RLS bypass) in prod — fix migration is drafted but not applied
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260519000003_invite_funnel_views.sql lines 33–93: views created without WITH (security_invoker = on). supabase/migrations/20260618000004_security_invoker_views_and_idempotent_tables.sql line 5 explicitly marked 'DRAFT — NOT yet applied to prod'. Views read from invites, session_events, raw_dumps, retention_events (all RLS-enabled tables). Currently views are GRANTed only to service_role (anon/authenticated revoked), so the security_definer risk is latent — it activates only if an errant future GRANT hits authenticated.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Latent: if a developer accidentally grants view SELECT to the authenticated role, the view bypasses underlying RLS and exposes cross-user invitee_user_hash, first_dump_at, d1_returned_at — PII correlation attack.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: A defense-in-depth gap. Not exploitable in current state but one errant migration away from cross-user data exposure.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Apply migration 20260618000004 to prod — one `supabase db push` command. The migration is already written and tested.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Very low. CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW with only the security_invoker option added — identical definition, service_role callers unaffected.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Integration test: authenticated role cannot SELECT from invite_funnel after migration. service_role can still SELECT.

mergedFindings.title: Clerk JWT verification omits audience (aud) claim check
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/clerk-verify.ts lines 64–72 (R1), 66–70 (R2/R3): jwtVerify called with only { issuer: env.CLERK_ISSUER } — the jose 'audience' option is absent. Clerk sessions include an aud claim set to the Clerk publishable key. Round 2 noted this is exploitable if staging and prod share the same Clerk issuer (same Clerk application), allowing a staging user's token on prod endpoints. Round 3 confirmed the same gap.
mergedFindings.userImpact: If staging and production share a Clerk issuer domain, a staging user's session token authenticates to production workers. In a single-app Clerk setup this is not exploitable — hence 'suspected' status.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Cross-environment or cross-app token acceptance. Standard JWT best practice requires audience validation.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add audience: env.CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY to jwtVerify options in clerk-verify.ts. Add CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY as a wrangler secret. Verify that Clerk issues a stable aud claim per frontend API key.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low. Tightens validation only.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: clerk-verify.test.ts: JWT with wrong aud returns null even with correct issuer and valid signature.
mergedFindings.dissent: Rounds 1 and 2 rated this P2. Round 3 rated it P3 (suspected, depends on Clerk config). Kept at P2/suspected because the fix is trivially low-risk regardless of exploitability.

mergedFindings.title: /partner/pair 6-digit pairing code has no per-attempt rate limit — brute-force feasible by authenticated attacker
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/router/partner.ts lines 102–134: pair() looks up the code with no attempt counter. workers/ai-proxy/src/index.ts lines 229–244: outer rate limit is 100/min keyed on attacker's own Clerk sub. CODE_TTL_SEC = 1800 (30 min). 100 req/min × 30 min = 3000 guesses against a 1M code space → 0.3% hit rate per victim during the active window. If victim regenerates the code multiple times the cumulative probability rises.
mergedFindings.userImpact: An authenticated attacker can pair with a victim's partner window without consent, gaining read access to the victim's intimate-window snapshot (mood, crisis flag, gone-dark status).
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Low-probability but high-sensitivity data exposure. The intimate-window holds the most personal data in the app (crisis boolean, mood, energy).
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add a per-code attempt counter in KV (key: pair:attempts:<code>). After 5 wrong guesses, mark the code burned regardless of TTL. Drop CODE_TTL_SEC from 1800 to 600.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low — additive KV counter; no schema change.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Test: 5 failed /partner/pair attempts on a code → 6th attempt returns 410 even before TTL expires.

mergedFindings.title: USER_HASH_SALT is optional with silent degradation — unsalted SHA-256 user identity hashes in prod if secret is unset
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/telemetry.ts lines 46–47: if (!salt) console.warn('[telemetry] USER_HASH_SALT unset — hashing userId unsalted'). Typed as USER_HASH_SALT?: string in EnrichEnv and IngestEnv. wrangler.toml has no USER_HASH_SALT entry in [vars] or secrets comment list. DEPLOY_TODO.md documents VITE_USER_HASH_SALT (different name) — naming inconsistency suggests the secret may not be set under the correct worker variable name.
mergedFindings.userImpact: If USER_HASH_SALT is not set, every user's telemetry identity hash is SHA-256(userId) — reversible by anyone with a Clerk user ID list via a lookup table. The 'anonymous' telemetry guarantee is broken.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Privacy guarantee failure on analytics tables. Changing the salt retroactively invalidates all existing hashes.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Run `wrangler secret list --name ollie-ai-proxy` to confirm. If unset, add the secret. Change the warning to a hard 500 on startup so misconfiguration is caught immediately rather than silently degrading.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low — fail-fast config check. Adding a salt now does not break existing rows (they retain old unsalted hashes); new rows get salted hashes.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Unit test: deriveUserHash with undefined salt produces a different hash than with a salt. Integration test: worker returns 500 on startup probe when USER_HASH_SALT absent.

mergedFindings.title: profiles table has active anon SELECT grant for a retired Supabase auth flow
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260518000001_profiles_anon_email_lookup.sql: grants anon SELECT on (id, email, salt, encrypted_server_pw) of public.profiles for the 'new-device sign-in' flow. packages/auth/src/index.ts now explicitly states it is 'ONLY the encryption layer' and no longer does any Supabase Auth or server-password logic. The anon grant remains active with no revoke migration.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Any unauthenticated caller can query /rest/v1/profiles?select=id,email,salt,encrypted_server_pw&email=eq.<email> and retrieve PBKDF2 salt and AES-GCM ciphertext for any user. Enables offline passphrase brute-force (mitigated by PBKDF2 iteration count but unnecessary exposure).
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Unnecessary pre-auth exposure of encrypted key material. The ciphertext is useless without the passphrase but the attack surface should not exist.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add migration: REVOKE SELECT ON public.profiles FROM anon; DROP POLICY IF EXISTS profiles_select_anon_recovery ON public.profiles — conditional on confirming no live code path calls /rest/v1/profiles pre-auth.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low if the new-device recovery flow is confirmed unused. Verify no E2E test or live code calls this endpoint before applying.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Confirm no app code or E2E test queries /rest/v1/profiles with anon key.

mergedFindings.title: Invite endpoint auth uses x-user-jwt header (non-standard) while all other endpoints use Authorization Bearer — Supabase fallback kept alive on invite paths
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/invites.ts lines 72, 220: req.headers.get('x-user-jwt'). All other authenticated endpoints use req.headers.get('authorization') with Bearer prefix. apps/native/src/api/workers.ts lines 507, 541 sends x-user-jwt. The verifyJwt function (invites.ts line 379) tries Clerk first then Supabase fallback — a Supabase-only JWT that Clerk rejects still passes auth on these two endpoints even after Clerk is fully deployed.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Header inconsistency means the Supabase fallback is structurally kept alive on invite endpoints. A leaked Supabase JWT that fails on /route/dump still works on /generate-invite. Increases the chance of a client bug where invite calls are sent without the correct header.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Migration-stall trap — invite endpoints never fully migrate to Clerk-only as long as the non-standard header is used. Two auth surfaces on the same two endpoints.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Rename x-user-jwt to Authorization in invites.ts and update apps/native/src/api/workers.ts to send Authorization Bearer. The verifyJwt function already handles both Clerk and Supabase from a single token string — only the header name changes.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Low. Client and server change in lockstep. No other callers of x-user-jwt found outside apps/native/src/api/workers.ts.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Confirm invite endpoints reject requests with x-user-jwt after migration to Authorization header.

mergedFindings.title: Telemetry tables (raw_dumps, enriched_signals, routing_cache) have no explicit REVOKE — future permissive grant would immediately expose cross-user data
mergedFindings.evidence: supabase/migrations/20260618000001 and 20260615000002_force_rls_and_grants.sql: raw_dumps, enriched_signals, research_corpus have no authenticated or anon policies — default-deny is correct by Postgres default (no RLS = deny when RLS is enabled). However no explicit REVOKE ALL FROM authenticated, anon exists for these tables, and no SECURITY.md documents the service-role-only intent. routing_cache and partner_* tables also lack explicit revoke.
mergedFindings.userImpact: Currently safe by default-deny. Any future accidental GRANT to authenticated immediately exposes all users' raw brain dumps and enriched signals to each other — highest sensitivity data in the app.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Defense-in-depth gap: relies on no errant GRANT rather than explicit revoke. These tables hold the richest user content.
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: Add a migration: REVOKE ALL ON raw_dumps, enriched_signals, research_corpus, routing_cache FROM authenticated, anon with an explanatory SQL comment that these are service-role-only tables. 2-line migration.
mergedFindings.riskOfFixing: Very low — REVOKE on already-denied roles is a no-op operationally.
mergedFindings.testsToAdd: Migration assertion tests: authenticated and anon roles cannot SELECT from raw_dumps, enriched_signals, routing_cache.

angleSummary: Security audit of Ollie monorepo (branch redesign/olive-neumorphic). Three rounds inspected workers/ai-proxy, workers/sentry-tunnel, apps/native (Tauri/React), packages/crypto, packages/notifications, supabase/migrations, and .env files. All critical findings are code-confirmed. Runtime gaps (migration application status, deployed wrangler secrets) flagged where applicable.

mergedFindings.title: /brain-dump and /v1/messages Anthropic proxy endpoints are completely unauthenticated
mergedFindings.evidence: workers/ai-proxy/src/index.ts lines 436–497: after all guarded routes fall through, /brain-dump and /v1/messages have zero JWT verification. Rate-limit key is req.headers.get('x-user-id') || req.headers.get('cf-connecting-ip') || 'anon' (line 443) — x-user-id is a plain request header, fully attacker-controlled. Every other expensive AI endpoint (/route/dump, /transcribe, /route/:module) has Clerk JWT enforcement. /brain-dump was never upgraded. The /v1/messages alias is still called by packages/api/src/anthropic.ts (routeViaHaiku).
mergedFindings.userImpact: Any internet caller who discovers the worker URL can POST arbitrary Anthropic API calls at Ollie's ANTHROPIC_API_KEY expense — no account needed. Rotating fake x-user-id values defeats the per-user rate-limit bucket entirely (10 req/min × N distinct keys). Attacker can also set x-user-id to a victim's Clerk ID to fill their rate-limit bucket (DoS on target user).
mergedFindings.smallestSafeFix: In workers/ai-proxy/src/index.ts, before the rate-limit block at line ~440, add the same T0_JWT_ENFORCED-gated Clerk JWT check already used in handleTranscribe (verifyClerkJwt, fail-closed, return 401 on missing/invalid JWT). Check whether packages/api/src/anthropic.ts sends a Bearer token before deploying — if not, migrate routeViaHaiku callers to /route/dump which is already auth-protected.
mergedFindings.technicalImpact: Unmetered Anthropic API spend. No audit trail for callers. Both endpoints forward the full caller-supplied body to api.anthropic.com with no model or token-count cap beyond a 1 MiB body limit.
